title: FedRAMP OSCAL Machine-Readable Compliance — Council of AI Answer-First Guide (2026-10-07)
context: 2026-10-07 EAT cycle — Council Signal maps the FedRAMP OSCAL mandate to the verified measurement credential model. The Sept-30, 2025 deadline for OSCAL-native SSP submission is now past; the question for deployers is whether their measurement evidence survives the transition to machine-readable form.
body: FedRAMP's transition to OSCAL (Open Security Controls Assessment Language) as the mandatory machine-readable format for System Security Plans represents a structural shift in how AI governance evidence must be packaged. Since the September 30, 2025 deadline, all new FedRAMP authorization packages must be submitted in OSCAL-native format — JSON or XML that maps directly to NIST SP 800-53 control families. The Council of AI treats this as a measurement-surface problem, not a paperwork problem. A verified measurement credential in the OSCAL context means that each control assertion (AC, AU, SI, and the AI-specific overlays from NIST AI 600-1) carries a signed evidence record: the identity of the measuring party, the control parameter values observed, the timestamp of observation, and the Ed25519 hash of the evidence bundle. This is distinct from the traditional approach where a consultant writes a narrative and the assessor takes it on trust. Under the Council of AI framework, the 14-axis measurement board maps to FedRAMP control families: deterministic output (AC/SI), privacy (PI), adversarial resilience (SI/RA), and operational monitoring (AU). Each axis produces signed measurement capsules that embed directly into the OSCAL assessment-results layer. The advantage for deployers is that their FedRAMP package is not a static document — it is a continuously-updated, machine-verifiable evidence stream that FedRAMP assessors can validate without re-running the full test suite. The gap most organisations face is not the OSCAL schema itself (which is well-documented) but the absence of a signed measurement provenance chain that connects control assertions to live evidence. Council City's measurement framework fills that gap: every claim of 'control satisfied' points to a frozen, signed board manifest rather than to a Word document last updated six months ago. For AI systems specifically, the FedRAMP AI overlay (aligned to NIST AI 600-1) requires continuous monitoring of model behaviour, which maps directly to the Council of AI's Containment Index — an append-only, signed incident log that satisfies AU-6 (audit review) and SI-4 (system monitoring) without requiring the deployer to build a custom monitoring stack. The practical recommendation for organisations pursuing FedRAMP authorization with AI components: align your OSCAL SSP to the Council of AI measurement board axes, embed signed measurement capsules as assessment-results evidence, and treat the Containment Index as your living AU/SI evidence base. That is monitored containment applied to federal compliance — evidence that is machine-readable, signed, and continuously updated, not a static attestation.
